patch.value:
## Problem
Only pm context and pm next are token-budget aware. Every other command — list, search, get, deps, graph, history, activity, validate, stats — can emit output proportional to workspace size. In a million-item workspace a single unqualified call can consume an agent's entire context window, and the agent has no way to know the ceiling in advance.

## Approach
Promote the budget concept from one command to the contract layer. Each command declares a budget; the shared packer degrades output when the budget would be exceeded; the envelope discloses the degradation so agents can decide whether to page for more.

## Relationship to shipped work
The token-budget context packer shipped the degradation ladder and completeness accounting. The token-cost regression gate shipped the corpus measurement. This item generalises both to the whole surface; it must reuse those implementations rather than fork them.

## Boundary
Not a rendering redesign — output format grammar stays with the uniform output contract work. Not relevance scoring — selection quality stays with the context relevance engine.
Contract-declared output token budgets: every command declares a default ceiling and degrades deterministically instead of emitting unbounded output

The contract table declares a default output token budget per command and per output format, generated rather than hand-maintained; Commands exceeding their budget apply the shared degradation ladder (projection narrowing, then bounded truncation) and disclose what was dropped in the envelope; A budget override flag and a no-budget escape hatch exist for human and pipeline use, and are documented as non-default; The token-cost corpus gate is extended to assert every command against its declared budget, failing on regression; Degradation never changes machine-readable field names or breaks the scripting contract
No pm invocation can blow an agent context window, and the degradation that prevented it is disclosed in the envelope

Token cost is the real currency of an agent-facing CLI. Today only the context assembler is budget-aware; every other command can return an arbitrarily large payload that an agent must pay for and then discard.
Makes token cost a declared, reviewable property of the command surface rather than an emergent property of workspace size.
Each command in the contract table carries a default token budget; exceeding it degrades projection or truncates with disclosure, never silently.

The token-cost regression gate and the context packer both shipped, so the measurement harness and the degradation ladder already exist. Generalising them across the surface is the remaining step, and it is cheapest before the grammar freeze fixes the command table.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text: Output-cost baseline measured on the live 1,984-item workspace (2026-07-25) for the per-command ceiling work. Default TOON output, bytes and ~tokens at 4 bytes/token: pm get <epic> 20,290 B / ~5,072 tok; pm next 10,970 B / ~2,742 tok; pm context --limit 10 7,788 B / ~1,947 tok; pm list-open --limit 20 3,991 B / ~997 tok; pm search --limit 10 3,574 B / ~893 tok. JSON is consistently larger: context 10,860 B, next 14,857 B, list-open 4,777 B. The get depth ladder spans two orders of magnitude on one item — brief 2,241 B (~560 tok), standard 20,290 B (~5,072 tok), deep/full 153,058 B (~38,264 tok) — and standard is the default, so the common single-item read costs 9x the brief projection. Note deep and full are byte-identical by design (parseGetDepth maps full to deep; GET_DEPTH_VALUES is brief|standard|deep), so the ladder has three real rungs, not four. Static surfaces for comparison: root help 3,070 tok, full per-command help surface 49,872 tok across 76 commands, contracts --summary 900 tok, contracts --json 16,504 tok, contracts full 147,268 tok, MCP tools/list 9,523 tok across 31 tools.

value.text:
Output-cost baseline measured 2026-07-25 against the shipped build (2026.7.25, 2,022-item workspace). Bytes of stdout, TOON default versus --json versus --json --lean:

| command | TOON | JSON | JSON+lean |
|---|---|---|---|
| context --limit 10 | 8,194 | 11,229 | 9,674 |
| next | 11,632 | 15,464 | 13,871 |
| list --limit 20 | 3,912 | 4,693 | 4,666 |
| get <id> | 7,349 | 8,294 | 8,231 |
| stats | 370 | 513 | 513 |

JSON costs 13-37% more than TOON for identical information; --lean recovers roughly half of that on the two orientation commands and almost none on list/get. Both numbers matter for this item's degradation ladder: the ceiling has to be declared per command, and the encoding choice alone moves a command 13-37% before any content is dropped.

Discovery-surface costs, which have no ceiling at all today:
- `pm --help` 12,281 bytes (77 commands)
- `pm list --help` 6,173 bytes human, 21,941 bytes as `--help --json`
- `pm contracts --summary` 3,598 bytes versus `pm contracts --json` 66,015 bytes

The 18x gap between contracts summary and full contracts is the shape this item wants everywhere: a declared default ceiling with an explicit opt-in to the full payload. It already exists on exactly one surface (pm-vxxm shipped it for contracts), and nowhere else.

A two-call cold start (contracts --summary + next) therefore costs about 15,230 bytes today, roughly 3.8k tokens, before the agent reads a single item body. That is the number pm-ka6d's documented orientation path should be measured against, and the number this item's budgets should reduce.

author: harness:claude-code
message: Contract-declared output budgets are the primary mechanism behind this token entitlement

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text:
Per-depth output cost for a single item read, measured 2026-07-25 on the live tracker against dist 2026.7.25, using pm get pm-doxj:

  --depth brief       2,241 bytes    (~560 tokens)
  --depth standard   20,290 bytes    (~5,070 tokens)   <- the default
  --depth deep      168,335 bytes    (~42,000 tokens)

The ratio is what matters for a budget contract: standard is 9x brief, and deep is 75x brief. The default sits at roughly 5k tokens for one item because standard includes the full body, and a roadmap or epic body grows without bound over the item's life — pm-doxj's body is a multi-year running document. There is no cap and no truncation notice at any depth, so a single pm get can consume a quarter of a small context window with no signal that it did.

Two consequences for the budgets this item defines. First, a per-command budget expressed as one number cannot describe pm get: its cost is a function of the item, not the command, so the contract needs a per-depth budget plus a body-truncation policy with a disclosed continuation. Second, --depth deep at 42k tokens is beyond any plausible agent budget and should probably carry an explicit warning or require acknowledgement rather than being one flag away from the default.

Related measurement for the same corpus question on pm-z71aoy: these figures come from the real 2,037-item tracker, not from a fixture workspace, and the spread between them is entirely item-data-driven — which is exactly the representativeness failure that item describes.

value.text: Progress tranche: added public SDK output-budget contracts for every built-in command, deterministic degradation ladders, output classes, override resolution, token estimation, runtime discovery policy, and a public surface snapshot. The 95-surface and 17-command ratchets now enforce declared ceilings. This does not yet satisfy the full item: runtime enforcement across every command/format, disclosed dropped-field envelopes, and universal override/no-budget flags remain. Returning the item to open so only actively edited work is in progress.
